assumptions: That customers were affected at all: no user-facing error reports or request-volume data were available, only the service's own latency warnings and timeout errors.
That the affected traffic was customer-facing purchasing traffic, inferred from the service name alone.

That impact started around 21:35 (first latency warning) rather than 21:37 (alert creation), and that it ended at or near 21:38 — the end timestamp is when the automated responder stopped, not an observed recovery. No log line or metric confirms the service recovered.

That the 21:34 deploy is the relevant change, on the basis that it was the only one recorded in the lookback window. A change made outside this service's change record (config, feature flag, dependency deploy) would not have appeared.
The error-rate figures cited in the investigation narrative (0.01 to 0.12) are treated as unverified: the incident record states metrics could not be read, and no log line contains them.
That no action was taken during the incident, so nothing in the system state was altered by the response and nothing needs unwinding.
input.executive_summary: Shortly after 21:35 UTC on 2 September 2026, the shop service began responding slowly, and within about two minutes a portion of requests were timing out rather than completing. Customers hitting the service during that window would have seen pages that hung and then failed. The automated responder opened an incident at 21:37, formed the same explanation three times — that a code release pushed a minute before the slowdown was responsible — and each time found no safe, reversible action it was permitted to take, because no rollback or equivalent undo was available to it. It therefore took no action at all and handed the incident to a human at 21:38. The 66 minutes-of-an-hour figure on the incident record (about four minutes wall clock, 21:37 to 21:38) measures how long the automated responder was working, not how long customers were affected: the degradation was already underway when the alert fired, and nothing in the record confirms when service returned to normal. Metrics for the period could not be read, so the extent of customer impact is not measured.
input.impact_weight_reason: This is a judgement, not a measurement. The only evidence bearing on it is the service name, io-shop, which suggests a customer-facing shopping path rather than an internal or administrative one. There is no route-level breakdown, no traffic or conversion data, and no metrics at all for the incident window — the error-rate figures quoted in the investigator's hypotheses (1% rising to 12%) do not appear in any log line read and were not confirmed against metrics. So we cannot tell whether the affected traffic was checkout (which would justify a weight near 1), browsing and listing pages (where many visitors would return later, justifying something well below 1), or a mix. 0.5 is the midpoint chosen in the absence of that evidence: it assumes roughly half of the interrupted requests represented revenue that was lost rather than deferred. If route-level traffic data can be recovered for 21:35–21:40, this number should be replaced rather than defended.
input.root_cause: Not established. The only change in the 24-hour lookback was a deploy of revision 9f4c1e7b2a3d5c8e1f0b6a4d2c9e7b5a3f1d8c6e to io-shop at 21:34, one minute before latency began climbing (220ms baseline → 1800ms at 21:36 → 5000ms timeouts at 21:37), so a regression in that revision is the leading hypothesis — but it rests entirely on timing: the logs name no dependency, pool, query or resource, no rollback was performed to confirm it, and a saturating downstream dependency or resource exhaustion would produce the same latency-led signature.
